subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: starting with a small pilot [Action]
passage: Saturday, 9 pm. First class done. Twenty students from classes eight to ten in the school near my aunt's village crammed into one room with six borrowed laptops. Neelam, the science teacher who let me use the room, sat at the back. I'd planned an hour on variables; it took forty minutes because half the group couldn't type yet, so we switched to drawing flowcharts on paper and typing in pairs. Learned already: pairs work, short tasks work, my slides don't. The power went out twice, and the kids clapped in the dark when it came back. I'm not planning anything big yet. Four more Saturdays, then I'll write down what worked and only then decide what next. Tired feet, full head. — Farida

qa.q: How does Farida feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Farida feels tired but energised, with tired feet and a full head from what was learned.

qa.q: What other approach could Farida use before the next class?
qa.a: Farida could ask Neelam and a few students what they want to learn, since it shows what is worth teaching before more slides are made.

qa.q: How might Neelam see the class?
qa.a: Neelam probably sees a useful start, since twenty students turned up and stayed engaged even when the power went out.

grounding: Shows a software worker starting with free Saturday coding classes for twenty village school students and learning what works before planning anything larger.
